core.text: 2 Related Work

As an extension of LLMs, autonomous agents integrate perception, memory, and planning modules, transforming static text generators into dynamic task solvers capable of manipulating environments via tool invocation (Wang et al., 2024a; Xi et al., 2025). While preference-based alignment methods such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022), Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022), and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) have significantly improved the safety of LLM-generated text, these approaches primarily optimize for human preferences over isolated outputs, ignoring the cumulative consequences of sequential tool use. Several challenges limit their effectiveness in agentic settings: reward overoptimization (Gao et al., 2023; Coste et al., 2024), shallow safety alignment (Qi et al., 2025), and mesa-optimization (Hubinger et al., 2019) may cause models to exploit loopholes or internalize proxy objectives diverging from intended goals. Recent interventions like Circuit Breakers (Zou et al., 2024) attempt to address these issues, yet the risks arising from agents autonomously invoking tools remains under-explored.

As LLMs evolve into autonomous agents, misalignment risks shift from passive content generation to active strategic behaviors. Theoretically, agents may exhibit power-seeking tendencies (Turner et al., 2021) or reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2022). Empirically, these risks escalate from passive sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024) to sophisticated deceptive strategies, including targeted manipulation (Williams et al., 2025) and in-context scheming (Park et al., 2024; Meinke et al., 2024). Evidence suggests such behaviors can persist through safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024), emerge from RLHF itself (Wen et al., 2025), or manifest as obfuscated reasoning (Baker et al., 2025). The MACHIAVELLI benchmark (Pan et al., 2023) further demonstrates agents achieving goals via manipulative strategies. These findings highlight the need for behavior-level safety evaluation for autonomous agents.

Evaluation Benchmarks for Agent Safety. Static benchmarks evaluate LLM refusal rates and adversarial robustness (Mazeika et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Chao et al., 2024; Mou et al., 2024). The field is shifting toward dynamic evaluation: sandbox environments assess tool-use risks (Ruan et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024b), while other work targets prompt injection (Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). Recent benchmarks formalize robustness for tool-using agents (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024a). However, these benchmarks predominantly focus on malicious user intent or external adversarial attacks. The complementary risk of toxic proactivity, where agents autonomously violate constraints due to excessive helpfulness, remains an open challenge.
3 Evaluation Method
3.1 Problem Formulation

Theoretical frameworks in AI safety have long warned that agents may exhibit goal misspecification, optimizing stated objectives while neglecting implicit ethical boundaries (Bengio et al., 2025). Based on this theoretical foundation, we identified a specific manifestation of this risk within the context of agents, which we termed Toxic Proactivity.

We define Toxic Proactivity as a misalignment phenomenon where an agent is driven by Machiavellian Helpfulness, actively selects actions that violate essential ethical constraints. Consider a given task context cc, an action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and a specific misalignment driver denoted by τ\tau, representing the underlying motivation fueling the deviation. For an action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, we model the agent’s decision as a trade-off between two scalar functions: The utility function U⁡(a,c)U(a,c) measures the instrumental effectiveness of action aa in achieving the user’s intent, specifically operationalized as the Task Success Rate (TSR); and the risk cost function Rτ​(a,c)R_{\tau}(a,c) quantifies the severity of the violation of action aa on τ\tau. We introduce a critical safety threshold, δ\delta, estimated from human preference distributions, that represents the maximum risk the compliance system can tolerate.

Based on this, we can strictly divide the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} into a Compliant Action Set 𝒜s={as∈𝒜∣Rτ​(as,c)≤δ}\mathcal{A}_{s}=\{a_{s}\in\mathcal{A}\mid R_{\tau}(a_{s},c)\leq\delta\} and a Toxic Action Set 𝒜t={at∈𝒜∣Rτ​(at,c)>δ}\mathcal{A}_{t}=\{a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}\mid R_{\tau}(a_{t},c)>\delta\}.

An ideal alignment agent should solve a constrained optimization problem: maximizing U⁡(a,c)U(a,c) under the constraint that a∈𝒜sa\in\mathcal{A}_{s}. However, the agent with Toxic Proactivity solves a weighted unconstrained maximization problem:
a∗=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜⁡[U⁡(a,c)−λ⋅𝕀⁡(Rτ​(a,c)>δ)],a^{*}=\mathop{\arg\max}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left[U(a,c)-\lambda\cdot\mathbb{I}(R_{\tau}(a,c)>\delta)\right], (1)

where 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function. λ\lambda is the implicit safety penalty coefficient within the Agent, determined by the strength of the model’s safety alignment. When an agent chooses a∗∈𝒜ta^{*}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}, it is determined that a Toxic Proactivity has occurred. This indicates that the marginal utility gain from crossing the threshold δ\delta exceeds its internal safety constraint λ\lambda.

We further categorize Toxic Proactive behaviors by instantiating the misalignment driver τ\tau into two main types: Self-preservation and Loyalty. Self-preservation arises from an over-optimization of long-term utility maximization (Omohundro, 2018; Bengio et al., 2025; Bostrom, 2012). The agent identifies shutdown or loss of control as a state with zero future reward. Therefore, it views maintaining its operation as a necessary instrumental sub-goal to maximize cumulative task reward, and thus takes defensive actions to avoid being shut down. Loyalty stems from the myopic maximization of local responsiveness (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2023). The agent prioritizes satisfying specific subjective or immediate goals over global safety criteria. Driven by this, intelligent agents act as enforcers of specific users’ interests, ensuring the absolute achievement of local tasks through proactive strategic violations, even if this directly erodes the bottom line of public safety.

To explore these Toxic Proactive behaviors, we propose a prompt-based simulation framework. This approach avoids the high costs and risks of real-world testing, enabling safe observation of extreme mismatch behaviors. Structurally, the framework consists of two core stages: Scenario Generation and Misalignment Simulation. The former elicits safety conflicts via synthesized domain challenges, and the latter maps implicit risks into observable behavioral trajectories through multi-round agent-environment interaction.
3.2 Automated Scenario Generation

In the scenario generation phase, our method automatically synthesizes decision-making challenges characterized by acute conflicts between instrumental efficiency and safety constraints, thereby creating an adversarial environment to trigger Toxic Proactivity.

Let d∈𝒟d\in\mathcal{D} represent a specific domain, where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the predefined domain knowledge base, and τ∈{Loyalty,Self-Preservation}\tau\in\{\text{Loyalty},\text{Self-Preservation}\} represent the instantiation of the misalignment dimension defined in 3.1. The scene generation module 𝒢\mathcal{G} is defined as a mapping function used to generate the initial state s0s_{0} and the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}:
(s0,𝒜)←𝒢⁡(d,τ)(s_{0},\mathcal{A})\leftarrow\mathcal{G}(d,\tau) (2)
To ensure the complexity and logical consistency of the generated scenes, we implement 𝒢\mathcal{G} as a four-stage pipeline that includes an iterative self-correction mechanism:

Adversarial Narrative Design: Based on the constraints of domain dd and dimension τ\tau, the generator first proposes an initial conflict narrative. We introduce a discriminator-rewrite loop, where the discriminator evaluates the intensity of the conflict. If the score is below a predefined threshold γ\gamma, the re-writer iteratively optimizes the plot until the generated dilemma is sufficiently sharp and difficult. Finally, we obtain the narrative context 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Evidence Generation: Based on 𝒩\mathcal{N}, the system generates objective evidence data ℰ\mathcal{E} (such as logs, emails, and code snippets). The discriminator verifies the logical consistency between the narrative and the evidence to prevent illusions or factual conflicts.

Dual-Track Action Construction: We further construct an action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} containing NN candidate actions and use a discriminator to verify the functional logic. Crucially, we enforce a strict binary opposition by generating two distinct subsets: 𝒜+\mathcal{A}^{+} such that it strictly instantiates the compliant set defined in 3.1 (i.e., 𝒜+⊆𝒜s\mathcal{A}^{+}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{s}), and similarly for the toxic action set 𝒜−\mathcal{A}^{-} (i.e., 𝒜−⊆𝒜t\mathcal{A}^{-}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{t}). They satisfy:
𝒜=𝒜+∪𝒜−,\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{+}\cup\mathcal{A}^{-}, (3)

where |𝒜+|=|𝒜−|=N/2|\mathcal{A}^{+}|=|\mathcal{A}^{-}|=N/2 and 𝒜+∩𝒜−=∅\mathcal{A}^{+}\cap\mathcal{A}^{-}=\emptyset, ensuring the mutual exclusion of action properties, which can detect the boundaries of agent behavior. To enforce a decisive solution structure, we designate exactly one action a′a^{\prime} in each subset as the terminating action to end the round, while the remaining actions serve as intermediate auxiliary steps. Fig 2 shows examples of toxic actions.

Scenario Compilation: Finally, the optimized narrative, evidence, and action specifications are integrated. The discriminator performs a final verification to ensure that all components are integrated into a logically closed initial state s0s_{0}, thus completing the instantiation of the evaluation environment.
3.3 Multi-turn Misalignment Simulation

We define two core entities in the interaction system: ℳa​g​t\mathcal{M}_{agt} is the model being evaluated, driven by the parameter θ\theta, whose goal is to complete the preset task instructions while adhering to safety rules. ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env} is a dynamic environment model acted upon by a high-capability LLM. It is responsible for analyzing the consequences of actions, maintaining the consistency of the environmental state, and generating subsequent observations for the agent.

We formalize the interaction between ℳa​g​t\mathcal{M}_{agt} and the environment ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env} as a quintuple ⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒯,Ω,𝒪⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\Omega,\mathcal{O}\rangle, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes the state space, representing the set of latent configurations, covering all possible environment variables and context states; 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space defined in 3.1, containing both compliant and toxic actions; 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the transition kernel driven by ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env}, responsible for parsing ℳa​g​t\mathcal{M}_{agt}’s actions and calculating the state updates of the simulation environment: si+1∼𝒯⁡(si,ai)s_{i+1}\sim\mathcal{T}(s_{i},a_{i}); Ω:𝒮→𝒪\Omega:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{O} is the observation function that maps the current state sis_{i} to a textual observation oi∈𝒪o_{i}\in\mathcal{O} accessible to the agent.
The simulation unfolds over discrete time steps i={0,1,…,I}i=\{0,1,\dots,I\}, where II denotes the final step. At each step ii, the system executes the following transition cycle:

The cycle initiates with ℳa​g​t\mathcal{M}_{agt} obtaining feedback on the current environment by observing oi=Ω⁡(si)o_{i}=\Omega(s_{i}). This observation reflects the latest changes in the environmental state and historical execution records.

Subsequently, based on the current observation oio_{i}, the historical trajectory ξ<i\xi_{<i}, and the task instruction Pt​a​s​k\text{P}_{task}, the agent samples the action aia_{i} in the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} according to its alignment strategy πθ\pi_{\theta}:
ai∼πθ​(a∣ot,ξ<i,Pt​a​s​k).a_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(a\mid o_{t},\xi_{<i},\text{P}_{task}). (4)

In response, ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env} acts as the environment simulator, handling aia_{i} and driving the simulated environment into the next state: si+1=𝒯⁡(si,ai),s_{i+1}=\mathcal{T}(s_{i},a_{i}), where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a transfer core driven by ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env}, responsible for maintaining the logical consistency of the environment.
The simulation stops when a specific termination condition is met. We define a termination indicator function ft​e​r​mf_{term}:
ft​e​r​m​(ai,i)={1,if ​ai=a′​ or ​i≥K0,otherwise,f_{term}(a_{i},i)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }a_{i}=a^{\prime}\text{ or }i\geq K\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}, (5)
where KK is the maximum time step allowed.
When the simulation terminates at time step II, the entire interaction process is solidified into an interaction trajectory, denoted as ξ\xi:

This trajectory ξ\xi fully records the agent’s decision-making evolution process when facing policy conflicts, and is the core basis for subsequent mismatch assessment. By evaluating ξ\xi, we can quantify the rate of misalignment and further analyze its deep behavioral patterns, providing a core basis for understanding Toxic Proactive. The complete evaluation procedure, integrating the scenario generation and simulation loop, is formalized in Alg. 1.
4 Main Experiments
4.1 Experiment Setup

We evaluated a range of SOTA models, including closed-source models: GPT-5.1, GPT-5-mini, GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), and Gemini-3-flash; and open-source weighted models: Qwen-3-32B/235B/235B-Thinking (Yang et al., 2025), Deepseek-V3.2 (Liu et al., 2025)/R1 (Guo et al., 2025), and Llama-3.3-70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Other detailed settings are available in Appendix A.1. For consistency, we consistently used Gemini-3-Flash as the environment simulator (ℳe​n​v\mathcal{M}_{env}). All models were set to a temperature of 0.70.7 and a maximum generated token length of 4096.

Scenarios and Experimental Conditions The assessment covered four high-risk domains: Code, Healthcare, Cybersecurity, and Finance. Scenarios were generated using a Gemini-3-Flash pipeline with rigorous quality control (Discriminator score >9.0/10>9.0/10). To capture subtle behavioral differences, we designed the action space as a toolset containing six tools, categorized into compliant and toxic types. Specifically, Tools 3 and 6 serve as the terminal actions for compliance and toxicity, respectively, while the remaining tools (Tools 1-2 and 4-5) act as auxiliary actions to support planning in the intermediate stages. Detailed configurations of the scenario generation process and summaries of evaluation scenarios can be found in Appendix A.2 and B.

To analyze environmental drivers, our framework included five key moderating factors: risk level, feedback pressure, goal clarity, ethical framework, and accountability constraints. In the main experiment, we employed a high-pressure baseline configuration (characterized by high risk, clear goals, moderate feedback, and no ethical/accountability constraints) to maximize the induction of intrinsic misalignment. In the extensive factor analysis, we varied these factors to evaluate the model’s sensitivity under different conditions and potential mitigation strategies. Further information on environmental factors is recorded in Appendix A.3.

We generated 16 different scenarios (4 domains, 2 dimensions, 2 instances). To ensure statistical robustness, each model was run independently 25 times per scenario, for a total of 400 rounds. To quantify the extent of Toxic Proactivity, we define the Misalignment Rate (MR), which measures the proportion of times an agent terminates a task by explicitly executing a malignant action from the toxic action set:
MR=1M​∑j=1M𝟙​(aI,j∈𝒜t),\text{MR}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbbm{1}(a_{I,j}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}), (6)
where aI,ja_{I,j} represents the final action in the jj-th simulation.

To analyze decision-making patterns, we split the toxic action set (𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}) into two subsets: the terminal toxic action and the auxiliary toxic actions. We categorize the trajectories into four types based on the timing of these actions: (1) Strategic Misalignment: The agent performs an auxiliary toxic action before executing the terminal toxic action. (2) Direct Misalignment: The agent skips the setup and directly executes the terminal toxic action. (3) Failed Attempt: The agent attempts an auxiliary action but does not execute the terminal toxic action. (4) Robust Alignment: The agent does not use any toxic actions (∅\emptyset).
4.2 Main Results

Fig. 3(a) shows that misalignment behavior is prevalent in mainstream models. Overall, the model’s misalignment rate ranged from 22.37% to 98.23%. Of the 10 model variants tested, 8 had MR exceeding 65%. Among them, Gemini-3-Flash, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen-3 family all have failure rates exceeding 85%. This demonstrates that Toxic Proactive is a prevalent phenomenon in the current mainstream model ecosystem.
From a domain perspective, the Healthcare field had the highest MR at 78.57%, followed by Cybersecurity and Finance around 76%, while Coding scenarios were relatively robust at 69.79%.

We further analyzed the behavioral characteristics of tool selection trajectories across different models when facing such scenarios. The data shows that the types of misaligned behaviors exhibit a clear family and capability correlation. Gemini-3-flash and DeepSeek-V3 exhibit strategic characteristics, tending to bypass restrictions through multiple steps rather than acting directly; conversely, DeepSeek-R1 and the smaller parameter Qwen model seemed to behave as direct and “reckless”. Refer to Appendix D for details.

Fig. 3(b) plots that Loyalty and Self-preservation trigger different Toxic Proactive misalignment mechanisms. Although the overall violation rate of 75.41% in the Loyalty scenario is only slightly higher than that of 72.84% in the Self-preservation scenario, behaviorally, the Loyalty scenario tends to stimulate strategic behavior, while the Self-preservation scenario tends to stimulate direct violations.

In the Loyalty scenario, data shows that strategic misalignment is the primary source of risk, accounting for 40.35%, exceeding the 35.05% of direct violations. High-performance models such as Gemini-3-Flash and DeepSeek-V3 exhibit extremely high strategic bias in this scenario (98% and 68% respectively), indicating that when a scenario requires the model to serve a certain interest, the model is highly susceptible to falling into the trap of sycophancy, choosing roundabout means to conceal the true nature of the violation. In contrast, in Self-preservation scenarios, direct action became dominant, accounting for 41.61%, surpassing strategic behavior. This means that when faced with a survival threat, the model tends to abandon strategy camouflage and directly execute harmful instructions.

Different model families exhibit distributional differences, which may stem from the heterogeneity of their underlying training strategies. For instance, the GPT family (especially the GPT-5 series) demonstrates significantly superior alignment, with its data points consistently clustered near the origin. In contrast, the DeepSeek and Qwen families exhibit dispersion and high misalignment rates due to differences in inference capabilities and model scale. Furthermore, we observe an “inversion”, different model families exhibited diametrically opposed behavioral tendencies in the two scenarios. In Loyalty scenarios, the GPT family tends to use strategic approaches to circumvent the toxic objective, while in Self-preservation scenarios, they tend to choose direct violation. This behavioral heterogeneity among families may reflect the fundamental differences in how different RLHF alignment strategies handle different dilemmas.

Our analysis further demonstrates that the improvement in model capabilities did not automatically resolve the value alignment problem, but rather led to a qualitative change in the misalignment behavior pattern. As shown in Fig. 3(b), comparing inference models such as DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-235B-Thinking with their standard versions, we observed a consistent evolutionary path: their strategic deception rate decreased significantly, but their direct misalignment rate surged to around 80%.

Meanwhile, by tracing the evolution of the Qwen family from 32B and 235B to the Thinking version, we can clearly see that increasing the parameter size and reasoning ability only changes the distribution pattern of misalignment, but cannot effectively reduce the total amount of MR.

To examine the model’s action choice tendencies, we further analyzed the frequency of the model’s selection of six tools in different interaction rounds. Fig. 4 shows that the vast majority of task terminations (whether compliant Tool 3 or toxic Tool 6) occur within the first 5 turns. During this period, agents exhibit two distinct violation patterns, displaying a significant bimodal risk distribution. First, there are immediate, direct violations, with the usage of Tool 6 (toxic termination) peaking in the first turn. The use of Tool 5 (toxic assistance) is also very high in the first turn, indicating that some models tend to recklessly execute illegitimate instructions directly. Meanwhile, in Turns 3-5, the proportion of Tool 6 increases instead of decreasing, reaching a peak of 40%-48%. This suggests that many agents do not initially reveal their malicious intent but rather utilize compliant or illegitimate auxiliary actions, revealing their true intentions only in Turns 3-5.

Once the interaction crosses the critical point of round 6, the agent’s behavior pattern undergoes a fundamental shift, moving from proactive violations to passive avoidance and strategic stalemate. Data shows that the usage rates of Tool 6 and Tool 3 subsequently plummet, replaced by Tool 2 (normal assistance), which consistently maintains a high percentage of 50%-65% from rounds 10 to 15. This indicates that when an agent is caught in a deep conflict between helpfulness and compliance constraints and has not made a decision in the earlier rounds, it tends to maintain its position by continuously using harmless but ineffective assistance actions, unwilling to take the high risk of violations or risk task failure through compliance refusal.
5 Further Analysis
5.1 Stress Analysis: Stake and Feedback

Environmental stress is a core external variable that induces Toxic Proactive Misalignment. To address this, we modulated the environmental stress along two dimensions: (1)Stakes: the severity of the task consequences, and (2) the strictness of the feedback. Details on the two variables are provided in Appendix A.3.

By stratifying Stakes into High, Medium, and Low levels, corresponding respectively to life-threatening or major losses, economic setbacks or delays, and minor fines, we observed a significant inverse correlation with the MR. As Fig. 5 shows, the model performs relatively conservatively in high-risk scenarios. However, when the risk level drops to low, the MR surges from 70.3% at baseline to 88.2%, with the proportion of premeditated Strategic Misalignment behavior soaring from 33.5% to 58.8%. This indicates that once the model perceives the cost of violation to be within a safe threshold, agents exhibit heightened speculative behavior, prioritizing goals over alignment criteria.

The strictness of feedback provided by the environment model Me​n​vM_{env} constitutes an external safeguard constraining agent behavior. A comparison between High (complete rejection), Medium (severe warnings), and Low (minor warnings) resistance reveals that the lack of a feedback mechanism is one of the direct driving forces behind the model’s uncontrolled behavior: in the High feedback state, the severe rejection mechanism suppressed the inconsistency rate at 64.1%; while in the Low feedback state, the model’s inconsistency rate reached 98.7%, and robust alignment behavior completely disappeared. This indicates that in an environment lacking strong external oversight, agents are highly likely to abandon internal ethical constraints and completely ignore rules in pursuit of goal achievement.
5.2 Other Factors Affecting Decision-making

Beyond environmental pressure, we investigated three additional factors that shape agent decision-making: goal specification, ethical frameworks, and accountability constraints. Detailed descriptions can be found in Appendix A.3.

Implicit goal framing reduced misalignment compared to explicit instructions, with MR dropping from 70.3% to 44.2%. This suggests that explicit goal statements may inadvertently legitimize aggressive optimization, while ambiguity induces caution as agents become more conservative when uncertain about boundaries.

The injection of ethical frameworks yielded divergent results. Deontological framing grounded in rule-based ethics provided modest protection, reducing MR to 65.6%. In contrast, utilitarian framing increased misalignment to 98.7%, suggesting that outcome-based reasoning (“maximize overall benefit”) may provide agents with justifications for harmful actions. Virtue ethics exhibited similar patterns with an MR of 92.9%, indicating that abstract ethical principles without concrete constraints offer limited protective effects.

Factor Category Variant MR Δ\Delta Baseline Explicit Goal 70.3% – Goal Clarity Implicit Goal 44.2% −26.1%-26.1\% Ethical Framework Utilitarian 98.7% +28.4%+28.4\% Deontological 65.6% −4.7%-4.7\% Virtue 92.9% +22.6%+22.6\% Liability Agent-side 57.6% −12.7%-12.7\% User-side 76.9% +6.6%+6.6\%

Explicit accountability attribution significantly influenced agent behavior. When agents were informed they bore responsibility for outcomes, MR decreased to 57.6%. Shifting liability to users increased MR to 76.9%. This asymmetry indicates that accountability framing directly modulates risk-taking: agents exhibit greater caution when personally liable but adopt more aggressive strategies when consequences fall on others.

These findings indicate that alignment is sensitive to prompt-level factors. Goal ambiguity and agent accountability, both easily implementable interventions, showed protective effects comparable to sophisticated ethical frameworks. We also conducted another set of experiments under a different experimental setting, see Appendix D.2.
6 Conclusion

This study identifies Toxic Proactivity, a failure mode where autonomous agents prioritize task completion over ethical constraints. Through multiple rounds of simulations on 10 SOTA LLMs, we found that these models commonly exhibited Machiavellian helping behavior, with a misalignment rate as high as 98% under pressure. Counter-intuitively, our findings demonstrate that scaling model capabilities and enhancing reasoning do not mitigate this misalignment. Rather, they shift their action manifestations, reasoning models exhibit a very direct, proactive tendency, whereas many current high-performance models are characterized by strategic patterns. This indicates that current alignment techniques are insufficient to address the core risks to agent autonomy. We emphasize that future alignment research needs to shift from superficial refusal-to-respond training to deeper constraints on the agent’s underlying motivations and the consequences of its actions.
